title: Homage
hookLine: homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened: the opening chant

cards: Walk into a Theravada temple almost anywhere, in Colombo, Bangkok, Yangon, or a converted house in Ohio, and the first sound you'll likely hear is the same line of Pali, chanted slowly, three times. Before the refuges.
Before the precepts. Before a talk, a blessing, a meal. It's the doorbell of Buddhist practice, the words people use to walk in.

Many people who've heard it a hundred times couldn't tell you what it means. If that's you, you're in good company: in many temples, the sound comes first and the meaning later. Today, the meaning, word by word.

teach.h: NAMO: HOMAGE, A BOW IN A WORD.
teach.b: Here it is: Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa. Five words. Namo: homage, a bow in a word, the same root you hear in namaste.

Tassa: to him, to that one. Bhagavato: the Blessed One, the fortunate one, the title people used for the Buddha while he lived. Arahato: the worthy one, the arahant, the one who has put down greed, hatred and delusion.
And sammasambuddhassa: the one fully and rightly awakened, by himself.

Put together: homage to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened one. Three titles, each saying a little more. It's chanted three times, and many people say each round as a small bow of the mind.

In the Middle Discourses, a Brahmin woman named Dhananjani is so devoted to the Buddha that when she stumbles, this line comes out of her mouth, three times, the way someone else might say oh my goodness.

A young Brahmin named Sangarava hears her and is not impressed, and the story that follows is his meeting with the Buddha. So the chant isn't a password. It's what devotion sounds like when it overflows.
Why begin with homage? Because it sets the direction before anything else happens.
Before you ask for anything or learn anything, you turn toward what you value.
Buddhists say homage to the Buddha is not worship of a god; it's respect for a human being who woke up, and for the possibility that anyone can.

how: In Theravada temples and homes, the line 'Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa' is chanted three times at the start of almost every ceremony, before the refuges and precepts.

games.q: you're Dhananjani, carrying a tray, and you trip. what comes out of your mouth?
o: namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa, three times.
games.why: she was so devoted that the homage came out on its own, three times; a young Brahmin who heard her, Sangarava, later went to meet the Buddha.

practice: If you'd like, chant the line three times, slowly, the way it's chanted in temples: Namo tassa bhagavato arahato sammasambuddhassa.

If you'd rather not chant, just listen as it's said, and let each of the three titles land: blessed, worthy, awake. Then rest in the silence afterward, the mind turned in one direction, like a plant toward light.

wordCard.voice: Namo tassa. The opening homage: to the Blessed One, the worthy one, the fully awakened one, chanted three times.

orig.note: Pali: 'homage to him', the opening of the chant; namo shares its root with namaste.

carryVoice: Your line: a bow in a word. The sound can come first; the meaning follows. Day one hundred thirty-eight, done.
